questions.question_text:
Consider a process executing on an operating system that uses demand paging. The average
time for a memory access in the system is M units if the corresponding memory page is
available in memory, and D units if the memory access causes a page fault. It has been
experimentally measured that the average time taken for a memory access in the process is
X units.

Which one of the following is the correct expression for the page fault rate experienced by
the process?
questions.explaination: The effective access time is $X = (1 - p)M + pD = M + p(D - M)$. Solving for $p$ yields $p(D - M) = X - M \implies p = \frac{X - M}{D - M}$.

questions.question_text:
Consider a system with 3 processes that share 4 instances of the same resource type. Each
process can request a maximum of 𝐾 instances. Resource instances can be requested and
released only one at a time. The largest value of 𝐾 that will always avoid deadlock is ____.
questions.explaination: For $n$ processes sharing $m$ instances of a single resource type where each process needs at most $K$ instances, deadlock is guaranteed to be avoided if $\sum_{i=1}^n (K - 1) < m \implies n(K - 1) \le m - 1$. Here $n = 3$ and $m = 4$, so $3(K - 1) \le 3 \implies K - 1 \le 1 \implies K \le 2$.

questions.question_text:
Consider a storage disk with 4 platters (numbered as 0, 1, 2 and 3), 200 cylinders (numbered
as 0, 1, … , 199), and 256 sectors per track (numbered as 0, 1, … , 255). The following 6
disk requests of the form [sector number, cylinder number, platter number] are received by
the disk controller at the same time:
[120, 72, 2] , [180, 134, 1] , [60, 20, 0] , [212, 86, 3] , [56, 116, 2] , [118, 16, 1]

Currently the head is positioned at sector number 100 of cylinder 80, and is moving towards
higher cylinder numbers. The average power dissipation in moving the head over 100
cylinders is 20 milliwatts and for reversing the direction of the head movement once is 15
milliwatts. Power dissipation associated with rotational latency and switching of head
between different platters is negligible.

The total power consumption in milliwatts to satisfy all of the above disk requests using the
Shortest Seek Time First disk scheduling algorithm is _______.
questions.explaination: Using Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) starting at cylinder 80: closest is 86 (diff 6, upward), then 72 (diff 14, downward $\implies$ reversal 1), then 116 (diff 44, upward $\implies$ reversal 2), then 134 (diff 18, upward), then 20 (diff 114, downward $\implies$ reversal 3), and finally 16 (diff 4, downward). Total cylinder distance $= 6 + 14 + 44 + 18 + 114 + 4 = 200$. Head movement power $= 200 \times 0.2\text{ mW} = 40\text{ mW}$. Direction reversals $= 3 \times 15\text{ mW} = 45\text{ mW}$. Total power consumed $= 40 + 45 = 85\text{ mW}$.

The read/write head is currently at cylinder 80 and moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The SSTF algorithm is used. The disk arm consumes 0.2 mW power for moving across one cylinder and 15 mW power each time it reverses its direction of movement. The total power consumed (in mW) to service all requests is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to deadlocks?

options.A: Circular wait is a necessary condition for the formation of deadlock.
options.B:
In a system where each resource has more than one instance, a cycle in its wait-for
graph indicates the presence of a deadlock.
options.C:
If the current allocation of resources to processes leads the system to unsafe state,
then deadlock will necessarily occur.
options.D:
In the resource-allocation graph of a system, if every edge is an assignment edge,
then the system is not in deadlock state.

questions.explaination: Circular wait is one of Coffman's four necessary conditions for deadlock (A is TRUE). If every edge in a resource-allocation graph is an assignment edge, no process is requesting any resource, so no process is blocked and deadlock is impossible (D is TRUE). In multi-instance systems, a cycle is not sufficient for deadlock, and unsafe states do not guarantee deadlock.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A:
The TLB performs an associative search in parallel on all its valid entries using page
number of incoming virtual address.
options.B:
If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit, but the subsequent
search for the word results in a cache miss, then the word will always be present in
the main memory.
options.C:
The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all
incoming virtual addresses.
options.D:
In a system that uses hashed page tables, if two distinct virtual addresses V1 and V2
map to the same value while hashing, then the memory access time of these
addresses will not be the same.

questions.explaination: An inverted page table organizes entries indexed by physical frames using a hash table with collision chaining. Because different virtual addresses can hash to chains of different lengths, the number of lookups varies, making statement C FALSE.

questions.question_text:
Consider four processes P, Q, R, and S scheduled on a CPU as per round robin
algorithm with a time quantum of 4 units. The processes arrive in the order P, Q, R,
S, all at time t = 0. There is exactly one context switch from S to Q, exactly one
context switch from R to Q, and exactly two context switches from Q to R. There is
no context switch from S to P. Switching to a ready process after the termination of
another process is also considered a context switch. Which one of the following is
NOT possible as CPU burst time (in time units) of these processes?
questions.explaination: With Round Robin scheduling and time quantum 4 for processes arriving as P, Q, R, S: in option D ($P=3, Q=7, R=7, S=3$), execution proceeds $P(3) \to Q(4) \to R(4) \to S(3) \to Q(3) \to R(3)$. This schedule incurs a context switch from $S$ to $Q$, from $Q$ to $R$, and from $R$ to terminate, but does not produce the required context switch counts. Hence, burst combination D is NOT possible.

Consider two files systems A and B , that use contiguous allocation and linked
allocation, respectively. A file of size 100 blocks is already stored in A and also in
B. Now, consider inserting a new block in the middle of the file (between 50th and
51st block), whose data is already available in the memory. Assume that there are
enough free blocks at the end of the file and that the file control blocks are already
in memory. Let the number of disk accesses required to insert a block in the middle
of the file in A and B are
A

questions.explaination: In contiguous allocation $A$, inserting after block 50 requires shifting blocks 51 to 100 right by one position (50 reads + 50 writes) and writing the new block (1 write), so $n_A = 50 + 50 + 1 = 101$. In linked allocation $B$, traversing to block 50 takes 50 reads; writing the new block takes 1 write; updating and writing back block 50 takes 1 write, so $n_B = 50 + 1 + 1 = 52$. Thus $n_A + n_B = 101 + 52 = 153$.

the page fault rate, defined as the ratio of number of page faults to the number of

Which one or more of the following need to be saved on a context switch from one
thread (T1) of a process to another thread (T2) of the same process?

However, each thread has its own private thread control block (TCB) maintaining its program counter, stack pointer, and general purpose CPU registers, which must be saved during a thread context switch.

questions.question_text:
Which one or more of the following options guarantee that a computer system will
transition from user mode to kernel mode?
questions.subtopic: System calls, processes, threads, inter-process communication
questions.explaination: A transition to kernel mode is triggered by traps, exceptions, or hardware interrupts. A Page Fault is a hardware exception handled exclusively by the OS kernel (C is true). A System Call issues an explicit software trap instruction switching the CPU to kernel mode (D is true). Standard user-space function calls and `malloc` execute in user mode without inherently causing a mode transition.

questions.question_text:
Which one or more of the following CPU scheduling algorithms can potentially
cause starvation?
questions.answer: A, C, D or C, D
questions.explaination: Priority Scheduling can cause starvation for low-priority processes if higher-priority processes arrive continuously (C). Shortest Job First (SJF) starves long burst jobs when short jobs arrive continuously (D). Under certain interpretations where FIFO queues suffer convoy effects or indefinitely waiting jobs in specific priority variants, FIFO was also credited, hence GATE accepted {C, D} or {A, C, D}. Round Robin provides bounded waiting and prevents starvation.

With counting semaphore $s=2$ (I-2), two threads can enter simultaneously; a decrement thread can read $X=10$, be preempted while all 5 increments and 2 decrements complete, and then write back $10-1 = 9$, repeatedly clobbering increments to achieve minimum $V_2 = 10 - 3 = 7$.

The nested loop accesses the array column by column ($j$ changes faster in $D[j][i]$), referencing all 32 pages sequentially in every column iteration. Because only 30 physical frames are available, LRU replaces the earliest page before a column pass finishes. Consequently, every page access across all 128 column passes causes a page fault: $128 \times 32 = 4096$ page faults.

questions.question_text:
Consider a computer system with 57-bit virtual addressing using multi-level
tree-structured page tables with L levels for virtual to physical address translation.
The page size is 4 KB (1 KB = 1024 B) and a page table entry at any of the levels
occupies 8 bytes.
The value of L is
.
CS
questions.explaination: Page size is $4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}\text{ bytes}$, which leaves $57 - 12 = 45\text{ bits}$ for the page table hierarchy. Each page table holds $\frac{4\text{ KB}}{8\text{ bytes}} = 512 = 2^9$ entries, so each level indexes 9 bits. The number of levels required to cover the 45 virtual page bits is $L = \frac{45}{9} = 5$.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?

options.A: Threads can only be implemented in kernel space
options.B: Each thread has its own file descriptor table for open files
options.C: All the threads belonging to a process share a common stack
options.D: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.subtopic: System calls, processes, threads, inter-process communication
questions.explaination: All threads of a single process share the same address space (code, global data, heap) and open files. Because they run within the same virtual address space without memory protection barriers between them, one thread can corrupt another thread's memory; hence they are by default not protected from each other (D is TRUE). Each thread maintains its own private stack and registers.

Similarly, only a Running process can initiate an I/O request and transition to Waiting; a Ready process cannot transition directly to Waiting (C is impossible).

questions.question_text:
Consider the following two threads T1 and T2 that update two shared variables
a and b. Assume that initially a = b = 1. Though context switching between
threads can happen at any time, each statement of T1 or T2 is executed atomically
without interruption.
T1 T2
a = a + 1; b = 2 * b;
b = b + 1; a = 2 * a;
Which one of the following options lists all the possible combinations of values of
a and b after both T1 and T2 finish execution?
questions.explaination: Initially $a=b=1$. Let statements be $T_1: [S_1: a=a+1, S_2: b=b+1]$ and $T_2: [S_3: b=2b, S_4: a=2a]$. Executing $T_1$ then $T_2$ yields $a=2, b=2 \to b=4, a=4 \implies (4, 4)$. Executing $T_2$ then $T_1$ yields $b=2, a=2 \to a=3, b=3 \implies (3, 3)$. Executing $S_1, S_3, S_4, S_2$ yields $a=2 \to b=2 \to a=4 \to b=3 \implies (4, 3)$. No valid interleaving can produce $(a=3, b=4)$.

Iteration 3 ($x=1$): each of the 4 processes forks (total 8 processes); all 8 print "hello" (8 prints) and decrement $x$ to 0, whereupon the loop ends. Total prints $= 2 + 4 + 8 = 14$.

questions.question_text:
Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of 2 KB. Assume that
both the physical and virtual addresses start from 0. Assume that the pages 0, 1, 2,
and 3 are stored in the page frames 1, 3, 2, and 0, respectively. The physical address
(in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address 2500 (in decimal format)
is _________
questions.explaination: With page size $2\text{ KB} = 2048\text{ bytes}$, virtual address $2500$ has virtual page number $\lfloor 2500 / 2048 \rfloor = 1$ and offset $2500 \pmod{2048} = 452$. Page 1 maps to frame 3. The physical address is $(\text{frame } 3 \times 2048) + \text{offset } 452 = 6144 + 452 = 6596$.

Consider a process P running on a CPU. Which one or more of the following events
will always trigger a context switch by the OS that results in process P moving to a
non-running state (e.g., ready, blocked)?

options.A: P makes a blocking system call to read a block of data from the disk
options.B: P tries to access a page that is in the swap space, triggering a page fault
options.C: An interrupt is raised by the disk to deliver data requested by some other process
options.D: A timer interrupt is raised by the hardware

questions.subtopic: System calls, processes, threads, inter-process communication
questions.explaination: When process P executes a blocking I/O system call, it must wait for disk transfer and is moved to the blocked state (A). When P experiences a page fault on a swapped page, it is put into the blocked state until disk I/O completes (B). Interrupts from other devices (C) or timer ticks (D) in preemptive systems might return directly to P after ISR handling if P has highest priority.

questions.question_text:
Consider a disk with the following specifications: rotation speed of 6000 RPM,
average seek time of 5 milliseconds, 500 sectors/track, 512-byte sectors.
A file has content stored in 3000 sectors located randomly on the disk. Assuming
average rotational latency, the total time (in seconds, rounded off to 2 decimal
places) to read the entire file from the disk is _________
questions.explaination: At 6000 RPM, one rotation takes $\frac{60}{6000} = 10\text{ ms}$. Average rotational latency $= 10/2 = 5\text{ ms}$. Transfer time per sector $= \frac{10\text{ ms}}{500} = 0.02\text{ ms}$. Time to access each random sector $= \text{seek} + \text{rotational latency} + \text{transfer} = 5 + 5 + 0.02 = 10.02\text{ ms}$. Total time for 3000 random sectors $= 3000 \times 10.02\text{ ms} = 30060\text{ ms} \approx 30.06$ seconds.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a disk with the following specifications: rotation speed of 6000 RPM, average seek time of 5 milliseconds, 500 sectors/track, 512-byte sectors. A file has content stored in 3000 sectors located randomly on the disk. Assuming average rotational latency, the total time (in seconds, rounded off to 2 decimal places) to read the entire file from the disk is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in range 29.50 to 30.50)

questions.question_text:
Consider a 32-bit system with 4 KB page size and page table entries of size 4 bytes
each. Assume 1 KB = 210 bytes. The OS uses a 2-level page table for memory
management, with the page table containing an outer page directory and an inner
page table. The OS allocates a page for the outer page directory upon process
creation. The OS uses demand paging when allocating memory for the inner page
table, i.e., a page of the inner page table is allocated only if it contains at least one
valid page table entry.
An active process in this system accesses 2000 unique pages during its execution,
and none of the pages are swapped out to disk. After it completes the page accesses,
let X denote the minimum and Y denote the maximum number of pages across the
two levels of the page table of the process.
The value of X+Y is ________
questions.explaination: Page size is $4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}$ bytes, PTE size is 4 bytes, so each page table holds $2^{12} / 4 = 1024$ entries. The process accesses 2000 unique pages. Minimum inner page tables $X$: $\lceil 2000 / 1024 \rceil = 2$ inner pages plus 1 outer page directory $= 3$. Maximum inner page tables $Y$: 2000 pages distributed across 2000 different inner tables, bounded by total possible entries in directory $= 1024$ inner pages plus 1 outer page directory $= 1025$. Hence, $X + Y = 3 + 1025 = 1028$.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a 32-bit system with 4 KB page size and page table entries of size 4 bytes each. Assume $1\text{ KB} = 2^{10}$ bytes. The OS uses a 2-level page table for memory management, with an outer page directory and an inner page table. The OS allocates 1 page for the outer page directory upon process creation. The OS uses demand paging when allocating memory for the inner page table. An active process accesses 2000 unique pages during its execution. Let $X$ denote the minimum and $Y$ denote the maximum number of pages across the two levels of the page table of the process. The value of $X + Y$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
Consider a demand paging memory management system with 32-bit logical
address, 20-bit physical address, and page size of 2048 bytes. Assuming that the
memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page
table?
questions.explaination: With a page size of $2048 = 2^{11}$ bytes, the page offset requires 11 bits. The 32-bit logical address is split into page number and page offset, so the page number has $32 - 11 = 21$ bits. Hence, the page table contains at most $2^{21}$ entries.

questions.question_text:
A computer has two processors, 𝑀1 and 𝑀2. Four processes 𝑃1, 𝑃2, 𝑃3, 𝑃4 with CPU
bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and
these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive
priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:
• 𝑀1 uses priority of execution for the processes as, 𝑃1 > 𝑃3 > 𝑃2 > 𝑃4, i.e.,
𝑃1 and 𝑃4 have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
• 𝑀2 uses priority of execution for the processes as, 𝑃2 > 𝑃3 > 𝑃4 > 𝑃1, i.e.,
𝑃2 and 𝑃1 have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
A process 𝑃𝑖 is scheduled to a processor 𝑀𝑘, if the processor is free and no other
process 𝑃𝑗 is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can
be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution
priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time
of the processes in milliseconds?
questions.explaination: At $t = 0$, $M_1$ takes highest priority process $P_1$ (burst 20) and $M_2$ takes $P_2$ (burst 16). At $t = 16$, $M_2$ frees up; among remaining processes $\{P_3, P_4\}$, $P_3$ has higher priority on $M_2$, so $P_3$ runs on $M_2$ ($t = 16$ to 41). At $t = 20$, $M_1$ frees up and executes $P_4$ ($t = 20$ to 30). Waiting times are: $P_1 = 0$, $P_2 = 0$, $P_3 = 16$, $P_4 = 20$. Average waiting time is $(0 + 0 + 16 + 20) / 4 = 36 / 4 = 9.00$ ms.

questions.question_text:
A disk of size 512M bytes is divided into blocks of 64K bytes. A file is stored in
the disk using linked allocation. In linked allocation, each data block reserves 4
bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block
contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of 1M bytes needs to be
stored in the disk. Assume, 1K = 210 and 1M = 220. The amount of space in bytes
that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is ______. (Answer in integer)

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee
questions.explaination: Block size is $64\text{ KB} = 65536$ bytes, with 4 bytes for pointer, leaving $65536 - 4 = 65532$ bytes of file data per block. File size is $1\text{ MB} = 1048576$ bytes. Number of blocks needed is $\lceil 1048576 / 65532 \rceil = \lceil 16.001037 \rceil = 17$ blocks. The first 16 blocks store $16 \times 65532 = 1048512$ bytes, leaving $1048576 - 1048512 = 64$ bytes stored in the 17th block. Internal fragmentation in the last block is $65532 - 64 = 65468$ bytes.

In linked allocation, each data block reserves 4 bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of 1M bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume $1\text{K} = 2^{10}$ and $1\text{M} = 2^{20}$. The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references
is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page
replacement algorithm is as follows:
The OS correctly predicts only up to next 4 page references (including the current
page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.
A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:
1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4.
If the system has three memory frames that are initially empty, the number of page
faults that will occur during execution of the process is ________ . (Answer in
integer)

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee
questions.explaination: Simulating the 3 frames with 4-step lookahead: 1 (fault, [1]), 3 (fault, [1, 3]), 2 (fault, [1, 3, 2]). At page 4 (fault): window is (4, 2, 3, 1), farthest is 1, so replace 1 -> [4, 3, 2]. Pages 2, 3 hit. At page 1 (fault): window (1, 2, 4, 3), replace 3 -> [4, 1, 2]. Page 2, 4, 3 (fault): replace 1 -> [4, 3, 2]. Total faults = 3 compulsory + 3 replacement = 6 page faults.

questions.question_text:
Processes 𝑃1, 𝑃2, 𝑃3, 𝑃4 arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds
respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively.
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling
policy. Ignore context switching times.
Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four
processes in milliseconds?
questions.explaination: Using preemptive SRTF: $P_1$ runs [0,2], $P_3$ runs [2,8] (finishes at 8, TAT = $8-2=6$). Then $P_4$ (remaining 9) runs [8,17] (finishes at 17, TAT = $17-8=9$). $P_1$ (remaining 8) runs [17,25] (finishes at 25, TAT = $25-0=25$). $P_2$ runs [25,38] (finishes at 38, TAT = $38-1=37$). Average TAT = $\frac{25 + 37 + 6 + 9}{4} = \frac{76}{4} = 19$ ms.

questions.question_text:
𝑃= {𝑃1, 𝑃2, 𝑃3, 𝑃4} consists of all active processes in an operating system.
𝑅= {𝑅1, 𝑅2, 𝑅3, 𝑅4} consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the
system.

The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

Assignment edges: 𝑅1 →𝑃1, 𝑅2 →𝑃2, 𝑅3 →𝑃3, 𝑅4 →𝑃4 (the assignment edge
𝑅1 →𝑃1 means resource 𝑅1 is assigned to process 𝑃1 , and so on for others)

Claim edges: 𝑃1 →𝑅2, 𝑃2 →𝑅3, 𝑃3 →𝑅1, 𝑃2 →𝑅4, 𝑃4 →𝑅2 (the claim edge
𝑃1 → 𝑅2 means process 𝑃1 is waiting for resource 𝑅2 , and so on for others)

options.A: Aborting 𝑃1 makes the system deadlock free.
options.B: Aborting 𝑃3 makes the system deadlock free.

Aborting 𝑃1 and 𝑃4 makes the system deadlock free.

questions.question_text:
A computer system supports a logical address space of 232 bytes. It uses two-level
hierarchical paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A logical address is divided into
a 𝑏-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page
table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses
eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.
The value of 𝑏 is ___________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.subtopic: Memory management and virtual memory: hierarchical paging
questions.explaination: For a $2^{32}$-byte logical address space with two-level hierarchical paging, page offset and page table index bits are derived from page size and entry size, yielding 11 bits for the first-level directory index.
